children: A Chinese deep-sea research team has identified an unusually metal-rich hydrothermal zone in the western Pacific, where preliminary tests found gold concentrations of up to 15.4 grams per tonne of ore. The same samples contained as much as 1,271 grams of silver per tonne.

The discovery was made during an 18-day scientific expedition in August. Researchers used underwater equipment to investigate a hydrothermal field in a western Pacific back-arc basin within China’s exclusive economic zone.

The newly identified site contains three large cone-shaped sulphide mineral structures. Researchers said the deposits are mainly made up of minerals such as chalcopyrite, pyrite and sphalerite, which can contain copper, iron and zinc.

Initial shipboard laboratory analysis showed unusually high concentrations of precious metals in some samples. Gold reached 15.4 parts per million (ppm), equivalent to 15.4 grams per tonne, while silver reached 1,271 ppm, or about 1.27 kilograms per tonne.
How did gold get to the ocean floor?

The answer lies in hydrothermal activity. Hydrothermal systems develop where seawater moves through cracks in the ocean crust and is heated by the hot rocks below. The water can dissolve and carry metals before rising back towards the seafloor.

When these extremely hot fluids meet colder seawater, minerals can precipitate and accumulate around the vents. Over long periods, this process can create massive sulphide deposits containing several metals.

The newly identified mineral zone is part of an area that researchers have been studying for years. Previous surveys found dozens of high-temperature hydrothermal vents at depths of around 700 to 1,500 metres. Some of the fluids emerging from the vents had temperatures above 315°C.
The latest expedition involved seven underwater vehicle dives and more detailed sampling to identify the new mineralised area.
Is this a giant gold mine?

Not yet. The reported 15.4 grams of gold per tonne refers to the highest concentration detected in some samples. It does not mean the entire deposit contains that concentration, nor does it establish the total amount of recoverable gold.
Researchers have identified significant resource potential, but further high-precision exploration will be needed to determine the size, composition and economic viability of the deposit.
Why is the discovery scientifically important?
The site could offer more than mineral resources. Scientists also found biological communities adapted to the extreme conditions around the seafloor hydrothermal system.

Studying these organisms could help researchers understand how life survives in environments with high temperatures, unusual chemistry and no sunlight. For now, the discovery is therefore both a potential deep-sea mineral resource and a natural laboratory for studying extreme life on Earth.

title: What is Gold doing under the Pacific? China finds 15.4g per tonne in deep-sea samples
